title: Would You Date Your Best Friend’s Ex? The Question That Exposes More Than Your Heart… It Reveals Your Character
paragraphs:
Would You Date Your Best Friend’s Ex? The Question That Exposes More Than Your Heart… It Reveals Your Character
Sometimes the greatest relationship dilemma isn't about love at all—it’s about loyalty, wisdom, forgiveness, and whether you're willing to honor Christ when your emotions say otherwise. Before you answer this question, let God examine not just who you love… but who you're becoming.
There are questions that instantly divide a room.
Would you forgive someone who betrayed you?
Would you marry someone with a difficult past?
Would you stay after being hurt?
But few questions stir emotions quite like this one:
"Is it wrong to date your best friend's ex?"
Some immediately answer, "Absolutely."
Others respond, "They're broken up. Nobody owns another person."
Many quietly whisper...
"It depends."
And perhaps that's exactly why this question deserves something deeper than a simple yes or no.
Because Scripture rarely asks only, "Is it allowed?"
Instead, God repeatedly asks something far more searching:
"Will this glorify Me?"
That question changes everything.
Because Christianity has never been about discovering the minimum requirements of holiness.
It has always been about becoming more like Jesus Christ.
That difference transforms how we approach relationships, friendships, forgiveness, romance, loyalty, and even our own desires.
The Bible never specifically says,
"Thou shalt not date thy best friend's ex."
No verse exists with those exact words.
Yet Scripture gives us timeless principles that reveal God's heart with remarkable clarity.
The Apostle Paul writes in 1 Corinthians 10:23:
The Greek word translated "build up" is οἰκοδομεῖ (oikodomei), meaning to strengthen, edify, construct, or build someone spiritually.
The issue isn't merely permission.
The issue is whether your decision strengthens or tears down the people God has entrusted to your life.
That is a radically different way of thinking.
Imagine two lifelong friends.
They laughed together as children.
They stood beside each other through heartbreak.
One defended the other when everyone else walked away.
They prayed together.
Celebrated victories together.
Cried together.
Then one relationship ended.
Months later...
or perhaps years later...
feelings unexpectedly developed between the remaining friend and the former partner.
Suddenly every emotion becomes tangled.
Love.
Guilt.
Fear.
Hope.
Confusion.
No one planned for it.
No one intended for it to happen.
Yet here they stand.
Is pursuing that relationship sinful?
Not necessarily.
But Scripture asks deeper questions before giving your heart permission.
Romans 14:19 says,
"So then let us pursue what makes for peace and for mutual upbuilding."
Peace.
Not merely personal happiness.
Mutual upbuilding.
Not merely personal fulfillment.
Christian maturity often means choosing what preserves relationships rather than simply chasing what satisfies emotions.
This is where our culture and Christ often move in opposite directions.
Culture says,
"Follow your heart."
Jesus says,
"Follow Me."
Those are not always the same path.
Jeremiah reminds us why.
"The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately sick; who can understand it?" (Jeremiah 17:9)
The Hebrew word translated "deceitful" is עָקֹב (ʿaqov), describing something crooked, insidious, or difficult to understand.
God never teaches us to blindly trust our emotions.
He teaches us to surrender them.
Sometimes what feels right isn't righteous.
Sometimes what feels loving isn't actually loving.
Love in Scripture is measured not by intensity but by sacrifice.
The Greek word ἀγάπη (agapē) refers to self-giving love that seeks another person's highest good before its own desires.
That changes the conversation dramatically.
Ask yourself honestly.
Would dating this person deeply wound your closest friend?
Would it reopen scars they're still trying to heal?
Would it fracture trust beyond repair?
Would it create unnecessary division within your Christian community?
If the answer is yes...
are you pursuing love...
or simply pursuing what you want?
Philippians 2:3-4 says,
"Do nothing from selfish ambition or conceit, but in humility count others more significant than yourselves. Let each of you look not only to his own interests, but also to the interests of others."
Notice what Paul does not say.
He doesn't tell believers to ignore their own desires.
He tells them not to let those desires become supreme.
That requires remarkable spiritual maturity.
Yet there is another side many people never consider.
Sometimes friendships have genuinely healed.
Sometimes years have passed.
Sometimes everyone involved has experienced forgiveness, growth, and emotional freedom.
Sometimes even the former friend gives sincere blessing.
Grace can accomplish what bitterness never could.
Because Christianity is built upon reconciliation.
Not permanent resentment.
Ephesians 4:31-32 says,
"Let all bitterness and wrath and anger and clamor and slander be put away from you... Be kind to one another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, as God in Christ forgave you."
The Greek word χαριζόμενοι (charizomenoi) literally carries the idea of graciously forgiving—extending undeserved favor because Christ first extended it to us.
Forgiveness, however, does not erase wisdom.
Nor does wisdom cancel forgiveness.
Both walk together.
If pursuing that relationship requires deception...
keeping secrets...
hiding conversations...
or hoping nobody discovers the truth...
your conscience may already be answering the question.
Jesus Himself declared:
"Whoever is faithful in very little is also faithful in much." (Luke 16:10)
Integrity matters long before wedding vows ever exist.
Relationships built upon concealed truth rarely produce lasting peace.
God is not honored merely by successful romances.
He is honored by holy ones.
This brings us to perhaps the hardest question of all.
Why do you want this relationship?
Loneliness?
Validation?
Chemistry?
Revenge?
Convenience?
Or because after much prayer, counsel, honesty, patience, and openness, you genuinely believe this honors Christ?
Psalm 139 records David praying,
"Search me, O God, and know my heart! Try me and know my thoughts!"
The Hebrew verb חָקַר (chaqar) means to search thoroughly, investigate deeply, examine completely.
David invited God into places most people spend their lives hiding.
That kind of honesty changes people.
Because God isn't merely interested in who you date.
He's transforming who you are.
Sometimes the greatest act of love is letting someone go.
Sometimes the greatest act of courage is having an uncomfortable conversation.
Sometimes the greatest act of faith is waiting longer than your emotions prefer.
Delayed obedience is difficult.
But obedience has never been wasted.
The greatest scandal in history was never about a complicated relationship.
It was the cross.
Humanity rejected its own Creator.
We betrayed the perfectly faithful Friend.
Isaiah foretold the suffering Messiah:
"He was pierced for our transgressions; He was crushed for our iniquities."
Jesus absorbed our scandal so that we could receive His grace.
This is why our theme is more than a slogan.
Every broken friendship.
Every failed romance.
Every guilty conscience.
Every poor decision.
Every regret carried for years.
Every relationship that ended in tears.
None of those stories are beyond Christ's redemption.
The Gospel never minimizes sin.
It magnifies the Savior.
Romans 5:8 declares,
"But God shows His love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us."
That is grace.
Undeserved.
Unearned.
Unmatched.
If you're facing this question today, don't begin by asking,
"What can I get away with?"
Ask instead,
"What most glorifies Jesus?"
Because one question seeks permission.
The other seeks transformation.
And only one of those will leave you with lasting peace.
Maybe this article exposed something you've been wrestling with in silence.
Maybe you have been the friend who felt betrayed.
Maybe you were the one who crossed the line.
Maybe you're standing in the middle of this very decision right now.
Wherever you are, Christ's invitation remains the same.
Come honestly.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Forgive where forgiveness is possible.
Pursue holiness over impulse.
Seek wisdom over urgency.
Choose faithfulness over temporary satisfaction.
Jesus does not merely repair broken stories.
He writes entirely new ones.

One surrendered decision today can rewrite generations tomorrow.
